notes.title: The Creator
notes.creator: Gareth Edwards
notes.review:
A beautiful, intimate piece of science fiction. Gareth Edwards allows us to think about the real nature of AI, pairing enormous images with a surprisingly human story about empathy, family, and what makes a person real.

The Creator puts on the screen what an imagery of what AI could become, a being capable of intelligence that grows beyond logic and rationality, but emotional, full of faith and love.  That humans may try to create a slave to be a servant for their needs, but will fail, and will create exactly what they fear the most: themselves, better, more united, cohesive, loving. 

When someone asks me what the future of AI is all about, I answer to watch this movie, because even though it is a simple script, it's magnitude, it's power, shapes my own personal vision of artificial intelligence is. It might be, for now, something we have on our computers and phones, but it will evolve to have a body and, with a body, it will grow to have their own society, their own beliefs, because, as God created us His image, we will create something that is our image, beings of belief, faith and emotional needs.

notes.title: Project Hail Mary
notes.creator: Phil Lord and Chris Miller
notes.review:
When I first heard of Project Hail Mary I thought to myself “so this is pretty much Interstellar for kids plus a funny little alien rock,” and I am not ashamed to admit I was absurdly wrong.

This movie was one of those movies that you finish watching and your mind keeps remembering the good moments, the intense moments, the sad ones. And I'll admit, became one of my favorite movies of all time.

The weight of your own life against the life of the whole world. That was something shocking to me because, mathematically, it’s simple, there’s no debate here, just plain facts: if it comes down to sacrificing one man to save over 8 billion, that’s a cheap price. But seeing Grace desperate to live his own life, even with nobody really there for him, and Eva rethinking her decision to force Grace into space while he is being chased, it brings up the question of how we see ourselves in comparison to others, and how important the whole context of humanity is even if there will be no more humanity to save.

Grace didn’t have anyone on Earth, he didn’t have a family, he barely had friends or even people who knew him; he was alone even though surrounded by people. And even so, he sobbed when Rocky offered him the possibility of going back home. And what does that mean exactly? We may be alone, but the feeling of being isolated, stranded, is something that goes against our nature as humans. We also get attached to spaces, so imagine leaving everything you know today, every little thing that brings you comfort, and throwing it away; you almost lose yourself, because the space we belong to is part of us. In other words: being alone and being without the world we grew up in breaks who we are.

Oh, I could stay here and talk all day about this. Seeing Grace present Earth to Rocky through images on the spaceship, and seeing him explain the little things we do and say, such as climbing up a tree, or going to the beach, “fist bumps,” hugs, and so on, it brings me joy and makes me remember that I am part of this context. It reminds me I’m alive in this scenario: I give hugs, I climb trees, I go to the beach. How amazing that is, and how strange it would be not to be able to be this alive, to live in a world this colorful and beautiful.

Seeing Grace run for his life, listening to Eva sing a song, or watching them talk by the sunset, watching Grace collect astrophage to save a humanity that couldn’t care less about who he is, it brings up the thought of how sophisticated and how intense life is, and how important it is to keep Earth safe and to protect humanity and our peace, so that dramatic actions, like Grace trying to save the world, are not for huge results, are to protect those small moments that build who we are as humans.

I loved watching this movie, from the bottom of my heart, it reminded me that sometimes we may be alone, but we need to keep doing our best, maybe sacrifice a little, to save humanity, to save the love we cultivate for one another, and to save this unique small blue planet we live on and ironically call Earth.

Thank you to Phil Lord, Chris Miller, and Andy Weir (I’ll be reading your book soon) for reminding me that being on Earth means way more than just news, catastrophe economy, politics and negativity. It means that we are alive, that we are privileged to be in such a wonderful world, with such amazing people around us, and that we have a duty to our planet and to our people if we want to preserve all the little and big things that make life worth living.

notes.title: Death Stranding 2
notes.creator: Hideo Kojima
notes.review:
A strange, patient journey about connection and the weight of carrying something for someone else. It asks you to slow down, notice the landscape, and find meaning in every small act of delivery. 

Death Stranding raises the most essential question of all: what are humans when we are alone? And the answer couldn't be simpler: We're doomed to become nothing.

notes.title: Witch Hat Atelier
notes.creator: Kamome Shirahama
notes.review:
Witch Hat Atelier is not just a story, it is an awakening back to the fantasy world, something I didn't feel ever since my first Harry Potter book, that excitement with a fantastical world and the fears of villains and spells of a world that only exists on these pages. 

This is my first ever manga, I've always had certain resistance in reading them for some reason, maybe for a certain prejudice. Now, at the end of each chapter, I find myself excited to see the next art that will be revealed, the next story that will be told.

Ms. Shirahama restored something that was long dead inside me, which is the very love for fantasy, the love for stories, books, the love of exploring a brand new world through reading, done in such a simple and tender way, through a story that isn't hard to understand, but it isn't simple to explain either. 

Another thing that I've been adoring from the story is the very thin line between the Witch Hat Atelier world and our own. I can clearly see resemblances between the Knights Moralis and the governments of our our world, the ethical laws that protect our world may be just like on Shirahama's world, something that, when questioned the existence you realize that you may want to cross to the brimmed caps side, and if you dig deeper, you may want to come back becoming a pointed hat, due to the fear of facing the truth. 

I'll continue writing this review in the given time, but until there, Ms. Shirahama, if you read this at any point: you restored my love for reading and for fantasy, a love that was long gone and now comes back to me like an old friend that I didn't see in a very long time.

notes.title: Black Myth: Wukong
notes.creator: Game Science
notes.review:
A majestic game steeped in Chinese mythology, a tapestry of tragic stories set in a world drowning in suffering, injustice, and poverty, while Heaven looks down and laughs from its privilege. Black Myth Wukong reaches far beyond its stunning aesthetics: beneath the spectacle lies a pointed critique of modern society. 

The source material for Black Myth is Journey to the West, a novel from 1592, only sharpens the irony, half a millennium later, the same rot it depicts still festers, and the game dares us to notice. That critique may not be the point, but it becomes impossible to look away from.

This game shows, through Wukong's eyes that, sometimes, to become great, and to overcome difficulties, challenges and complications, you need to fight your way through it and humbly learn through several errors made again and again.

notes.title: Hollow Knight
notes.review: A quietly devastating world that rewards attention. Hallownest feels hand-drawn, haunted, and full of little discoveries—the kind of place that stays with you long after you put the controller down.

notes.title: Deus Negro (Black God)
notes.creator: Neimar de Barros
notes.review:
Deus Negro (literally "Black God") is a poem by Neimar Barros in which the lyric self recounts his life as a man who looked down on the Black community, mistreating them, hating them, practicing racism as if it were natural. Upon arriving at the gates of Heaven, he sees, seated on the throne, a Black God. To his dismay, he must now spend eternity with a God cast in the very image of the thing he hated most his entire life, reminding him that, if he had treated all black folks as his equal, as his brothers and sisters on this Earth, he wouldn't have to live with such burden of hate on the afterlife. 

Barros shows us that hatred toward any race is like planting a seed that will not grow in this life. The more you cultivate it, the more accustomed you become to the practice. But the harvest comes in the afterlife, when you realize that the ones you mistreated never deserved it, that you were the one who caused their suffering, the reason for their misery, and that they may be the very image of God. The savior turns out to be the one you wronged, and so you are left to depend on their mercy.

notes.title: Final Fantasy XVI
notes.creator: Square Enix
notes.review:
Final Fantasy XVI was the first game in the franchise I ever played and, I'll admit, it wasn't quite my cup of tea. Even so, I recognize and respect the craft behind it and the success it earned. With that said, let's get into the review.

FFXVI is, undoubtedly, a mesmerizing game. It boasts beautiful environments, a solid story, and awesome boss fights, all elevated by an amazing score from Masayoshi Soken, the composer behind several other Final Fantasy soundtracks.

I loved every single fight cutscene: cities crumbling, powers erupting through the air, the tension at its absolute peak, Clive and Joshua pouring their hearts into the battle. That's exactly why I can't fully dislike this game. The combat gave me a great time, and the visuals left my jaw on the floor. The catch is that, for me, those scenes are most of what the game has to offer.

What cost it 2 stars in my review comes down to one thing: the stretches between boss fights were a slog. I spent countless hours bouncing from "go talk to John Doe" to "now investigate this" to "go talk to Jenny Doe," and it dragged my excitement from an absolute high down to sheer boredom, buried under political exposition I just couldn't bring myself to care about (which is totally fine, by the way, since everyone has their own taste in games). Honestly, I'd happily replay it if it were a straight boss rush that cut all the "political blah blah blah."

My second gripe is again down to personal taste: there's simply too much happening on screen. As much as I enjoyed the boss fights, there came a point where I was basically fighting light and explosions. I could barely make out the enemy's shape, defending and dodging on pure instinct after memorizing the patterns. I loved the fights where the enemy stood clearly in front of me. But in battles like the one against Ultima, I couldn't feel the tension because I couldn't actually see it, lost in a storm of damage numbers, explosions, and attack names. I don't think this is a flaw in the game so much as a trait of the genre. It's perfectly fine, just not for me.

A couple of other things are worth pointing out. FFXVI is, without a doubt, a pointed critique of how we treat the world and the "power" handed to us as a species. We take too much, cutting deep into nature's core, and that's exactly what the game explores. In its world, magic is the very thing corrupting nature, we're the ones responsible for that damage, and it's on us to fight back. I also loved how it handles bloodlines, nobility, and power. I could almost hear the writers saying, "we live this every day and do nothing, but in Final Fantasy we can fight it." That made me want to keep playing, because I wanted to bring justice to the weak with every bit of power I had.

In sum: a great game with gorgeous scenery and superb music, held back by uneven pacing that's either overwhelming climax or none at all, plus far too much clutter on screen in some boss fights. A genuinely successful game. Not for me, but kudos to the devs.

notes.title: The Egg
notes.creator: Andy Weir
notes.review:
This short story by Andy Weir was, for me, something I stumbled into completely out of the blue. For some reason I'd wandered onto a kind of sketchy blog while researching, and I found an article talking about a story called "The Egg." I was instantly hooked. "The Egg? What could this possibly mean?" And by the time I finished reading, I was in absolute shock with myself.

For those who don't know it, "The Egg" is about a man who dies and finds God waiting in front of him — a character I'd describe as rather funny, very human. God explains that the man is, after all, just an "egg," destined to reincarnate again and again until he matures enough to become equal to God himself. The twist is that every human who has ever existed is that same man, living in a different timeline and a different life.

What shocks me most is how brilliantly the story escalates. You start reading expecting something shallow (it's only a short story, after all) and you finish realizing that even the most selfish person alive has a reason to show love to everyone around them. Through Weir's lens, you are everyone, and everyone is you, so the very least you can do is treat yourself with respect, love and kindness. 

Another idea that blew my mind: if God really did make us capable of reincarnation — let's assume that's true for a second — it would take enough lifetimes to populate the entire world before any of us could truly grow, become better, and reach that so-called "Nirvana," that "God" state of mind.

An amazing story I didn't know I needed to read, even as a Christian. Phenomenal.

notes.title: Politics, Power and the End of the World
notes.creator: PeaceMonk
notes.review:
In case you, my reader, don't know: October is around the time of elections in Brazil. It's when the speeches about the "future of the country" begin (the talk of alliances with other nations, the expansion of power) and I'd like to give my take on it.

We live in a world of globalization, full of connection, steeped in a deep immediacy where everything is due yesterday. People are scared of how fast technology is growing; they're frightened of what the powerful could do with it — or already do. And for many, choosing the right politician feels essential to the progress of the country. But here is my opinion: politics is long gone, and what remains are only personal interests, the interest of the few, that laugh of their own nation.

This might stir some resistance in you as you read it. "Are you crazy? We live in a democracy — it doesn't work like that!" Do we? Everywhere we look, we don't see politicians, and it's been like that for a while. We see people who, in one way or another, drain resources toward their own pockets, their own interests, the preservation of their power and their beliefs — not the will of the people, not the good of the people. And some countries, without pointing fingers, also make sure to expand their reach well beyond their borders.

I lost faith in politics years ago. These are the words of a man who no longer believes any politician can make a difference, and who thinks the only difference that can be made must be made by the citizens themselves. How? I don't know. I don't think it's healthy to put everyone in control, but it isn't healthy to have no one in control either.

"So what are you suggesting? Communism? Libertarianism? Pick a side!" This is not a monochromatic debate, get over sides. What I'm suggesting is this: if politics is meant to work, the current way isn't working. The power politicians hold today only proves they've inherited far too much of it. They sit in positions where they control justice, taxes, borders, rights, and all citizens can do is watch the decisions get made every four years or so. That's assuming the elections aren't corrupted in the first place.

As Plato argues in The Republic, only those who do not seek power are qualified to hold it. He warned that people driven by a hunger for authority will use power to feed their own egos and desires. And over the past few centuries, democracy has evolved into exactly what Plato feared: ego, power, and desire.

This system — the way things are being run now — doesn't just affect our rights, our freedom, our borders. It affects the fate of the whole world. Because the people making these decisions, the ones with both hands on the wheel, are steering us toward the cliff with their foot on the gas and no intention of stopping.

The world needs change — but not the change we already know, not the kind revolutionary parties demand, not the world George Orwell imagined in 1984 or the one Isaac Asimov once dreamed up in Foundation. This is not science fiction. This is not a political novel. This is reality. 

Politics will only work when it truly serves the people, not when the people take it into their own hands through a "comuna," and not when every institution collapses. It will work only when countries stop obsessing over expanding borders, over data centers, over wars for conquest and prestige, over wars fought to prevent other wars. 

Politics is corrupted. It's rusty, moldy, and old, and it hasn't changed because the few who hold power are the same few who rule through threat and fear. Progress and peace will only come when politics is no longer about the ego of the few, but the will of the many.

(cover arts by Max VOAO)
